newsitem.title: THAILAND: Economic woes drive Thai stocks to 5-1/2 yr low.
newsitem.headline: Economic woes drive Thai stocks to 5-1/2 yr low.

text.p: Thai stocks fell to their lowest close in 5-1/2 years on Tuesday as concerns over the sluggish economy and anticipation of weak corporate earnings growth sparked fresh sales, traders said.
The key SET Index, which has been battered by a series of economic problems, dropped 2.55 percent to end at 643.28 points -- its lowest close since November 1, 1991.
Brokers said the market was not likely to improve in the near-term.
"Overall I see sentiment remaining bearish. Most people are already pessimistic," said Thanawat Patchimkul, analyst at Seamico Securities.
The fall was mainly brought on by jitters over the slowing economy's short and medium-term prospects, traders said.
Private economists project economic growth will slow to about five percent this year -- its lowest level in a decade.
Traders say the lower growth expectations and few clear signs of a quick recovery from the economic downturn sparked sales across the board.

"I think there is some evidence that the economy is bottoming out but it also seems that the recovery will not be strong and may not translate into earnings growth in key stocks," said Supavud Saicheua, head of strategy at large local broker Phatra Thanakit Plc.
The ailing finance sector, hit by worries of weak loan quality, investment portfolio losses and low broking revenues, dropped 4.54 percent.

"If the recovery is not very strong, some financial institutions will remain saddled with a larger proportion of non-performing loans, whereas a stronger recovery would help their loan situation," Supavud said.

The central bank's commitment to defending the currency means interest rates, which at a minimum 12.75 percent are among the highest in the region, cannot be cut enough to stimulate growth in the economy, analysts said.
Economists remain concerned about the country's export performance and some now feel the Bank of Thailand's 1997 target of 7.7 percent growth in exports may be over optimistic.

Those fears were heightened by market talk that the national minimum wage could be increased by 12.50 percent and make the already struggling, labour-intensive export industries less competitive with lower-wage regional competitors, traders said.

Communications stocks dropped 5.13 percent. Brokers said the decline was heightened by some foreign brokers' recommendations to decrease weighting in mobile operators which face increasing competition in a more liberalised telecommunications market. ($1 = 26 baht)
